structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father's advice to reserve judgment, which made him a confidant to others but left him disillusioned by the moral chaos he witnessed after returning from the East; he singles out Gatsby as the sole exception, admiring his extraordinary capacity for hope. In the spring of 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg, renting a modest bungalow between two grand estates, and feels isolated until a stranger asks him for directions, granting him a sense of belonging. That evening, he drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a Yale acquaintance, where he meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker lying motionless on a couch; during dinner, Tom passionately endorses the racist book 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' while Daisy and Jordan respond with detached irony, and a telephone call from Tom’s mistress in New York is met with Daisy’s forced cheerfulness and her bitter confession that she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool.' Afterward, as Nick prepares to leave, Daisy and Tom mention rumors of his engagement to a woman out West, which he denies, and later, alone on his property in West Egg under a bright summer night filled with insect sounds and distant frog calls, he sees Gatsby standing on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light at the end of a dock, before Gatsby vanishes.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate valley of ashes where they disembark and walk to George Wilson’s run-down garage to meet Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress; Tom insists Nick accompany them to New York, and they take separate train cars to avoid social exposure. In New York, Myrtle buys a dog, changes into a cream chiffon dress, and takes Nick and Tom to her rented apartment on the top floor of a building at 158th Street, where she invites her sister Catherine and the McKees; as alcohol flows freely, Myrtle boasts about meeting Tom on a train while pretending to be intimidated by his dress suit, and Catherine claims Myrtle and Tom plan to divorce their spouses and marry, falsely stating Daisy is Catholic and opposes divorce; the gathering descends into chaos as Mr. McKee attempts sketching guests, Mrs. McKee fixates on portrait opportunities, and Myrtle’s demeanor shifts from raw energy to exaggerated hauteur; the party collapses when Tom, enraged by Myrtle shouting Daisy’s name, strikes her across the face and breaks her nose, prompting frantic efforts to clean the blood with Town Tattle, after which Nick leaves with Mr. McKee, who offers a vague lunch invitation, and later finds himself exhausted on a bench at Pennsylvania Station waiting for the 4 a.m. train.

structure.title: III
characters_present: the drunk man in the library
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway arriving at Jay Gatsby’s mansion on Long Island late Saturday evening by car, invited by a formal note, where he finds a wild, opulent party in full swing—guests arrive by Rolls-Royce, station wagon, and motorboats, swimming, dancing under colored lights, and drinking champagne while rumors circulate about Gatsby’s mysterious past, including claims he killed a man or was a German spy. Despite wandering among strangers and meeting Jordan Baker, Lucille, Mr. Mumbles, and a drunk man in the library who is astonished to find Gatsby’s books are real, Nick Carraway does not meet Gatsby until midnight, when the man he had been conversing with at a table reveals himself to be Gatsby, whose unnervingly reassuring smile and formal mannerisms leave a strong impression; Gatsby invites him to ride in his new hydroplane the next morning. As the party descends into chaos—with drunken women weeping, marriages fracturing, and a coupé crashing outside—Nick Carraway observes Gatsby remain detached and sober, privately speaking with Jordan Baker, who later whispers something 'amazing' without elaborating. The chapter closes with Nick Carraway leaving to find the crashed coupe’s bewildered occupant claiming he wasn’t driving, while Gatsby stands alone on his porch, formally bidding farewell under a faint moon. In a reflective interlude, Nick Carraway describes his daily life in New York: working at the Probity Trust, lunching with clerks, studying investments in the Yale Club’s library, and walking home along Madison and Fifth Avenues, haunted by loneliness; he reconnects with Jordan Baker in midsummer, becoming disillusioned after learning she cheated in a golf tournament and lied about damaging a borrowed car, yet still affirms his belief that he is one of the few honest people he knows, despite being emotionally tied to a woman back home.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a sprawling, chaotic party filled with guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, arriving by car and engaging in absurd rumors about Gatsby’s identity, while incidents like Clarence Endive fighting a bum in the garden and Ripley Snell being run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s automobile underscore the revelry’s hollow excess; later that day, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with nickel accents and a three-noted horn, inviting him to lunch and recounting an elaborate, inconsistent personal history—including Oxford education, European aristocratic life, and a Montenegrin medal—as he reveals his intent to make a request regarding Jordan Baker; at noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsiem, whose cuff buttons are made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and later confesses that Gatsby fixed the 1919 World Series, before Gatsby vanishes after spotting Tom Buchanan; in a reflective flashback, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay and Lieutenant Gatsby in Louisville in October 1917, followed by Daisy’s extravagant wedding to Tom Buchanan, her drunken breakdown on her wedding day over a three-hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar pearl necklace, and their subsequent life in Chicago, until six weeks prior when the name Gatsby triggered Daisy’s recognition of the officer from her past; finally, riding in a victoria through Central Park at twilight, Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he now seeks Nick Carraway’s help to invite Daisy to tea at his neighbor’s house, prompting Nick Carraway to shift focus to Jordan, drawing her closer as they pass the lights of Fifty-Ninth Street.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy evening in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion illuminated but empty, with only the wind causing the lights to flicker; Gatsby, visibly anxious, invites Nick to Coney Island or a swim and awkwardly offers him a side business tied to Wolfsheim, which Nick declines. The next day, rain prompts Gatsby to send a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn, and he arrives for tea in a white suit, trembling with nerves; when Daisy arrives by car with her chauffeur Ferdie, Gatsby is paralyzed, nearly knocking over a mantel clock, but after an agonizing silence, Daisy weeps and Gatsby radiates joy, inviting her to tour his mansion. As the rain clears, they walk to the estate through the big postern, admiring its feudal silhouette and floral scents—jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate—while noting the eerie silence inside; Gatsby shows Daisy opulent rooms, including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, and encounters Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas doing liver exercises. In his study, Gatsby displays his vast collection of monogrammed shirts—silk, linen, flannel—in coral, apple-green, lavender, and faint orange—causing Daisy to collapse into tears; Gatsby laughs hysterically, emotionally drained. Later, he points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, now symbolically hollowed by her presence, and shows her photographs of Mr. Dan Cody and his youthful self in yachting gear, along with newspaper clippings about her; a phone call about Detroit is abruptly ended. Daisy marvels at pink clouds over the sea and jokes about placing Gatsby inside one. Klipspringer is summoned to play piano poorly but is ordered to continue; Gatsby lights Daisy’s cigarette with a trembling match, and they sit apart in shadowed seclusion as Nick observes Gatsby’s quiet doubt that reality can match his idealized dream of her, before leaving them absorbed in each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, baffled by wild rumors about his identity, prompting a reflection on Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who transformed himself after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht on Lake Superior and boarding the Tuolomee, where he served for five years in multiple roles before being left with nothing but an inherited identity after Ella Kaye seized Cody’s fortune. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled by the unexpected arrival of Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit on horseback; Gatsby nervously invites them to stay for drinks and supper, but they coldly decline, excluding him despite the woman’s earlier invitation. Later, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy dances with him but expresses discomfort at the vulgarity of West Egg’s crowd, while Tom accuses Gatsby of being a bootlegger and Daisy fabricates a story that he owns drugstores; afterward, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway his desperate hope that Daisy will tell Tom, 'I never loved you,' so they can erase five years of separation and reclaim the idealized moment when he first kissed her under the moonlight, believing he can repeat the past.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting, having replaced his original servants with reclusive relatives of Wolfsheim; tension erupts when Daisy kisses Gatsby in front of Tom, who reacts with stunned disbelief and reveals he has investigated Gatsby’s background, dismissing his claim of attending Oxford. The group departs for town in separate cars—Daisy and Gatsby in Gatsby’s yellow vehicle, Tom driving Nick and Jordan in the blue coupé—stopping abruptly at Wilson’s garage under the faded eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, where a sickly Wilson reveals he plans to move away with Myrtle and is suspicious of her secret life, while Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife. At the Plaza Hotel in mid-afternoon, a dramatic confrontation unfolds: Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim through drugstores, and Gatsby demands Daisy declare she never loved Tom; she falters, admitting she once loved both men, before Tom asserts his dominance and orders them back to Long Island in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle Wilson is struck and killed by a speeding car that flees the scene, witnessed by Michaelis, who finds her lifeless in the road with severe chest trauma and a torn shirtwaist; Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Wilson hysterical over her body, and Tom, shaken upon recognizing Myrtle, denies involvement, insisting his blue coupé was with him all afternoon. That night, Gatsby emerges from the shadows at the Buchanans’ house to confess to Nick that Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle and that he will take the blame, while Nick slips inside to witness Tom and Daisy quietly united over cold food and ale, leaving Gatsby alone in the moonlight, still watching over Daisy’s house.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected after Daisy briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light. They search the dusty, musty rooms for cigarettes, encountering a ghostly piano, while Gatsby refuses Nick Carraway’s urgent suggestion to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal, clinging to the belief that Daisy will choose him. Gatsby recounts his youth as a penniless officer who misled Daisy about his social standing and his later time with Dan Cody, which shaped his idealized vision of her. In a flashback, Gatsby traveled by day-coach to Louisville on his last army pay, walking the streets where he and Daisy had been together, desperately reaching for the fading memory of their love as the train departed. On the same morning, Gatsby refuses to drain his unused pool, and later, after instructing the butler to bring any calls to him at the pool and retrieving a pneumatic mattress from the garage, he disappears among yellowing trees. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and delusion after Myrtle’s death, discovers a new dog-leash on her bureau, declares 'God sees everything' while staring at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, and travels on foot to West Egg, learning Gatsby’s name. At four a.m., gunshots are heard; Gatsby’s body is found floating in the pool with the mattress drifting nearby, and Wilson’s body lies in the grass beside him, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the chaotic aftermath at his mansion, where police, photographers, and curious onlookers swarm the grounds while false testimony from Catherine erases Daisy’s involvement and brands Wilson a madman. Despite desperate attempts to reach Daisy and Meyer Wolfshiem—via phone, letter, and butler—Nick Carraway receives no response, and Wolfshiem declines involvement, citing business and shock. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and bundled in a cheap ulster, overwhelmed by his son’s grand estate; he shares a tattered copy of Hopalong Cassidy containing Gatsby’s childhood self-improvement schedule, revealing the boy’s earnest ambition. As the funeral approaches, nearly all of Gatsby’s acquaintances refuse to attend—Klipspringer calls only to request his tennis shoes, and Wolfshiem declines out of personal principle—leaving only Gatz, the Lutheran minister from Flushing, Nick Carraway, and a few servants. At five o’clock in a thick drizzle, a procession of three cars—motor hearse, limousine, and station wagon—arrives at the cemetery, where the owl-eyed man, whom Nick Carraway had previously seen marveling at Gatsby’s books, unexpectedly appears, wiping rain from his glasses to view the grave and quietly calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Afterward, Nick Carraway reflects on his nostalgic train rides to the Midwest, contrasting the authentic winter beauty of Chicago’s Union Station with his distorted memory of West Egg as an El Greco nightmare; he meets Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man and accuses him of dishonesty, prompting his admission that he is too old to deceive himself about honor. He later encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car, justifying it as retribution for Myrtle’s death while expressing distress over abandoned dog biscuits; Nick Carraway shakes Tom’s hand, seeing him as a child. Finally, alone in Gatsby’s abandoned mansion at night, Nick Carraway erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps and walks to the beach, meditating on the lost natural wonder that once enchanted Dutch sailors and drawing a parallel to Gatsby’s futile chase of the green light, symbolizing the receding American Dream.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg on Long Island, seeking opportunity in the bond business and renting a modest home next to the lavish mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, arrogant, and unfaithful—Nick is introduced to the decadent world of East Egg’s old money elite, as well as the reckless excess of Gatsby’s Saturday night parties. He also becomes romantically entangled with Jordan Baker, a cynical professional golfer, while growing increasingly fascinated by Gatsby’s mysterious persona and his quiet obsession with Daisy. Gatsby, it emerges, is not the aristocrat he appears to be but James Gatz, a poor North Dakota farm boy who reinvented himself after meeting the wealthy yacht owner Dan Cody, shaping his entire life around the dream of reclaiming a lost love with Daisy from five years prior.

As Nick becomes Gatsby’s confidant, he learns that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be near Daisy’s dock, where a green light symbolizes his unattainable ideal. With Nick’s help, Gatsby reunites with Daisy in a tense, emotional meeting that reignites their connection, but the illusion begins to unravel when Tom Buchanan confronts Gatsby at the Plaza Hotel, exposing his bootlegging ties and undermining his social legitimacy. Daisy, unable to fully renounce Tom, admits she once loved both men, shattering Gatsby’s fantasy of erasing the past. The confrontation ends with Daisy driving Gatsby’s car back to Long Island, where she accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress. Though Daisy is behind the wheel, Gatsby takes full blame, determined to protect her. Meanwhile, Myrtle’s grieving husband, George Wilson—led astray by Tom’s lie that Gatsby owned the car and was responsible for her death—tracks Gatsby down, believing him to be both a murderer and a lover who betrayed Myrtle.

In the aftermath of Gatsby’s murder at his pool—shot by Wilson before Wilson turns the gun on himself—Nick Carraway is left to arrange a funeral for a man whose glittering world evaporates in death. Despite Gatsby’s countless party guests and acquaintances, nearly all abandon him: Jordan Baker breaks off their relationship, Meyer Wolfsheim refuses involvement, and even Klipspringer calls only to retrieve his tennis shoes. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives from Minnesota, proud yet heartbroken, revealing a childhood scrapbook filled with self-improvement goals that mirror Gatsby’s relentless ambition. As Nick reflects on the hollow morality of the East, he confronts Tom Buchanan, who coldly justifies his role in the tragedy, and finally walks alone along the beach, meditating on the green light Gatsby once reached for—the symbol of a dream as lost and unreachable as the original promise of America itself. Nick, disillusioned but alive, resolves to return to the Midwest, having witnessed the collapse of illusion beneath the weight of wealth and desire.
